sections.history: Keezhaiyur lies in the Chola country north of the Kaveri, in the Mayiladuthurai region, and its Shiva temple is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, sung as Tirukkadaimudi in the Tevaram hymns of Sambandar. The village name is traced to the kiluvai tree beneath which Shiva is said to have appeared, in time softened from Kiluvaiyur to Keezhaiyur. The shrine's own name is explained in more than one way. Some read Kadaimudi as a softened Sadaimudi, the matted locks of Shiva, while the Lord's other name, Anthi Samrakshaneeswarar, speaks of the protector who keeps watch as the day ends. The temple has been tended through the medieval and later centuries; the founding patron is not firmly recorded.
sections.architecture: The sanctum of Kadaimudinathar faces west, a less common orientation among Shiva temples, and the goddess Abirami, also called Abhiramavalli, is likewise enshrined in a west-facing shrine of her own. Around the main sanctum are shrines to Nataraja, to Bhairava and to the Tevaram saints who carried the Shaiva faith into Tamil song. The plan follows the familiar Dravidian scheme of enclosure, sanctum and goddess shrine, kept up by the devotion of the village rather than by any royal monument. Finer details of its towers and halls were not verified.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of Brahma, cursed by Shiva for his pride, who came in search of release. Beneath a kiluvai tree he found a self-manifested lingam and worshipped it with devotion until the burden of the curse was lifted; the tree is said to have given the place its name. A second memory belongs to the sage Kanva, who worshipped the Lord here and bathed in the nearby Kaveri. The spot where he is remembered to have attained liberation is still called Kanva Mahan Thurai. Together the stories speak of a Lord who receives the proud once they bow, and who is found simply, beneath a tree, by those who seek him.
sections.festivals: The two principal festivals are Arudra Darisanam, honouring Nataraja in the month of Margazhi (December or January), and Karthikai Deepam, when lamps are lit in the month of Karthikai (November or December). Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come to Keezhaiyur for the stillness of a Tevaram village rather than for crowds. The west-facing sanctum draws the devotee into a different rhythm of approach, and many pause at the shrines of Nataraja and Bhairava before turning to the goddess Abirami in her own west-facing sanctuary. Those who know the legend of Brahma often sit a while beneath the temple's trees, thinking of the kiluvai under which the Lord first revealed himself. The temple is a short way from the village bus stop, and the surrounding countryside near the Kaveri adds to the quiet.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; published timings differ, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Keezhaiyur is in Tharangambadi taluk, Mayiladuthurai district, and is reached by road from Mayiladuthurai or Sirkazhi; the temple stands about 2 km from the Keezhaiyur bus stop. Mayiladuthurai Junction is the nearest major railway station, and Tiruchirappalli is the nearest large airport, well over 100 km away. Hiring a car from Mayiladuthurai or Sirkazhi is the most convenient way to reach the village.
